subject: Phase E — Unified Field Assistant — interaction design pressure test

user_context.primary_user: Paul — owner-steward, two modes: (1) mobile-in-field, voice-first, walking, single-hand, half-attention; (2) desktop-at-home, planning/reviewing, both hands, full attention.
user_context.secondary_user: Mom — co-steward, leisure-reading mode, bed-with-coffee or evening-wind-down posture, one-handed, half-engaged. Make-or-break user for the project overall.
core_jobs_to_be_done: Capture an observation fast while looking at the thing (Paul, mobile)
Ask the property a question and get a grounded, place-anchored answer (Paul, both modes)
Notice what is worth noticing today on this land (Mom, leisure-read; Paul, desktop)
Invest finite time well — know what is worth doing this month without the place becoming work (joint JTBD)
user_context.context_of_use: Top-of-page surface, above all main cards, below dashboard strip. Replaces the Phase D Quick Capture textarea. Visible on every page load, every device. Phone (~390px) is the dominant device for Paul-in-field; phone is also Mom's only device, in bed.
assumptions_made: Mom's adoption of the assistant is not yet validated behaviorally — her use mode and willingness to type questions to an AI is inferred from the field-journal leisure-read framing, not observed.
Paul-in-field voice-first usage is inferred from the brief; not yet observed in this surface.
The dashboard's current visual rhythm (cards as journal-pulls, quiet palette) is the visual baseline the new surface must coexist with.

principles_applied: Make every surface read at half-engagement (tate-tracker.md)
Glyphs follow the journal voice, not the dashboard voice (tate-tracker.md)
Strip teases, card holds (tate-tracker.md) — applied inversely: the new surface must not break the contract by withholding what it just did
Meet the user at the action (cross-project.md)
Norman — feedback, mapping, visibility of system state

Nielsen — Visibility of system state, Match between system and the real world, User control & freedom, Recognition rather than recall, Aesthetic & minimalist design, Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors

findings.observation: The 'classify-first, then act' (Option A) intent-routing pattern hides a real failure mode: when the classifier is wrong, the wrongness is invisible until the user notices the entry didn't land — or worse, lands as something it isn't. Three concrete failure shapes: (a) 'the laurel by the spring opened today' classified as Question (because it ends ambiguously and the model leans toward conversation), so it never enters the journal and Paul thinks he saved it; (b) 'when does the laurel usually open?' classified as Statement and saved as a meaningless observation that pollutes the journal; (c) Ambiguous path saves AND asks — which means Paul gets a follow-up he wasn't expecting AND has an entry in the journal he may not have wanted. The user has no visibility into which mode they're in *until after the model has committed*. That is a Nielsen 'Visibility of system state' failure in the most consequential moment of the flow.
findings.user_impact: Paul in the field, half-attention, voice-dictating: he says a thing, hears a 'saved' cue, moves on. The entry was misrouted, but he won't know until evening when he scrolls Field Notes and finds a question masquerading as an observation — or worse, doesn't find his observation at all because it got routed to chat. Field-journal trust erodes the first time this happens. For Mom, who is more likely to ask questions than save observations, a misclassified question saved as a junk entry teaches her the journal is noisy and she stops opening it.
findings.principle_invoked: Norman — feedback and visibility of system state; Nielsen H1 (visibility) + H3 (user control)
findings.recommendation:
Don't classify first and commit silently. Three moves, in order of preference:

(1) **Show the routing decision in the surface as it happens** — the moment classification returns, the surface visibly transitions to one of three states with a quiet but unmistakable cue: a small leading glyph or color band that says 'noted' (statement, green-tinted), 'asking' (question, neutral), or 'noted, with a question' (ambiguous). The label is the journal-voice version of the routing — never 'classified as Statement'. This is the minimum visibility bar.

(2) **Make the routing reversible for ~5 seconds.** A tiny inline affordance under the routed entry: 'Save instead' on a question that was routed to chat, 'Ask instead' on a statement that was routed to journal. Quiet text-link weight, never a button. After 5s it fades out and the routing is committed. This handles the ~5-10% misroute rate without making the user wait for a confirmation step on every turn.

(3) **Bias the classifier toward 'save' on ambiguity.** Of the three failure modes above, (a) — failing to save a real observation — is the worst because it loses data the user thinks they captured. Failing to give a conversational reply is recoverable (the user can re-ask). Losing an observation is not — the user has already moved on physically. Bias accordingly.

The pattern Paul should NOT reach for: a pre-classification mode toggle (Save / Ask buttons). That's the productivity-app pattern. It violates 'Friction kills' and it announces the AI machinery in a place the field-journal frame should hold. The unified surface is the right product call; the visibility gap is what needs the fix, not the unification.

findings.observation:
Save-success has no in-surface evidence. Phase D had this same issue and it survived into Phase E unaddressed. Today's behavior: user hits Save, textarea clears, entry appears in the Field Notes card *which is below the fold on every device*. On a 390px phone, the Field Notes card is roughly 1.5-2 viewport heights below the capture surface — the user has to scroll past Weather, Plants, Wildlife, Sky, and Place cards to see their entry land. On desktop the Field Notes card is also below the fold of attention because cards expand downward.

The failure is doubled for Phase E because there are now THREE possible save outcomes (statement saved, question replied, ambiguous saved+asked) and only one of them surfaces evidence in the current surface (the question reply). Statement saves are silent except for the textarea clearing — which is indistinguishable from 'I accidentally hit clear' or 'the network failed and my entry vanished.'
findings.user_impact: Paul in the field, voice-dictation, half-attention: dictates an observation, hears nothing back, moves on. He has no in-the-moment confirmation that the property received what he said. Over a week of use this becomes 'I'm not sure if it's actually saving things' — and either he stops trusting the journal or he develops a compensating behavior (scrolling down to check every time) that breaks the half-engagement contract. For Mom: she sees the textarea clear and assumes she did something wrong.
findings.principle_invoked: Norman — feedback (the most fundamental usability principle); Nielsen H1 (visibility); Tate-Tracker 'Make every surface read at half-engagement'
findings.recommendation:
Show the saved entry IN the unified surface, not just down in the Field Notes card. Concrete pattern:

**The surface should grow upward with a brief, low-decoration trace of what just happened.** After save, the textarea clears and a single line appears above it (or pinned just above the input field) showing: the entry as plain text, prefixed with a quiet journal-voice timestamp ('A moment ago · ') and followed by the classified category in italic gray once the async classify returns ('(birds)'). The line is non-interactive. It persists until the next turn, then it gets pushed up and the new turn's line takes its place. After ~4-5 turns the oldest fades. This gives Paul in-surface continuity AND solves the multi-turn chat-layout problem (F4) with the same pattern.

**Critically: the trace is the journal voice, not the chat voice.** It does NOT read 'Saved!' with a green check. It reads 'A moment ago — saw a Ruby-throated at the feeder · birds'. The trace IS the field journal happening in real time, not a confirmation toast.

**For Mom-mode (less technical, less aware of AI plumbing):** the trace doubles as the obvious cue that 'this is the journal I'm writing.' She doesn't need to know about classification to read the line.

**Empty-state of the trace area:** one quiet italic line — same register as the existing 'No entries yet' empty state in the Field Notes card. Probably the existing Field Notes intro line, lifted up: 'A place to set down what you saw this week.' That gives the surface a self-explaining empty state.

This pattern also solves the 'save-success' problem for the existing Phase D textarea retroactively. Ship F2 even if F1 is deferred.

findings.observation:
The unified surface, as currently scoped, would break the 'Strip teases, card holds' contract — but in a new way the principle didn't anticipate. The Field Notes card stays as the browse surface (correct). The unified surface is now BOTH the entry-point AND the live record of what just happened (per F2). Mom in bed glances at her phone — the unified surface shows the most recent turn. She taps. Where does she go? Currently: nowhere; the surface is the entire surface. The Field Notes card down below is a separate trip. There's a missing affordance from 'I saw the trace of my most recent observation up top' to 'show me the full journal.'

Separately: the surface duplicates today-line behavior in a way that wasn't designed for. The existing today-line is a proactive opener at the top of the dashboard. The unified surface sits directly below the dashboard strip and above main cards. Two evocative top-of-page surfaces with different voices and behaviors will read as competing for the same role.
findings.user_impact: For Mom: the unified surface is a smart-looking thing she may not know what to do with — she came to read about her place, not to talk to her place. If the empty state of the surface invites her to type, she'll close it. If it shows her something to read (recent observations, today-line, recent ask), she stays. For Paul: visual confusion between 'where the today-line lives' and 'where the assistant lives' will need a layout decision now, not later. For both: the missing 'go to full journal' affordance is the 'meet the user at the action' failure — the surface presents activity without offering the obvious next move.
findings.principle_invoked: Strip teases, card holds (tate-tracker.md, inverted-application); Meet the user at the action (cross-project.md)
findings.recommendation:
Two moves:

(1) **Add a quiet 'see the full journal' link** in the unified surface's footer area when there are recent entries traced in the surface. Text-link weight, journal voice ('See the full journal' or 'All entries' — content-steward call). Clicking expands and scrolls to the Field Notes card. This is the Phase E version of the strip-tile → card contract.

(2) **Decide explicitly where today-line lives in Phase E.** Two options: (a) today-line moves INTO the unified surface as the initial state — the surface opens with today-line as the journal voice's proactive read, the user types into it, and the surface becomes the conversation+today-line in one. (b) today-line stays where it is, the unified surface starts empty with the lifted Field Notes intro. Option (a) is more ambitious and consolidates two top-of-page voices into one (good); option (b) is safer and clearer (also good). My read: (a) is the better long-run shape because it makes the unified surface immediately useful even to a user who never types — Mom can open the page, read the today-line, never interact, and the surface has done its job. But (a) requires deciding what happens when today-line is stale or absent. Worth a Paul-level decision before build.

findings.observation:
Multi-turn chat layout at 390px is a real constraint that the brief acknowledges but doesn't solve. The dominant pattern in chat UIs is paired bubbles (user-right, assistant-left) growing downward into a scrollable container. That pattern is wrong here for three reasons: (a) it imports the messaging-app register, which fights the field-journal frame (Tone-coherence across all chrome — this is a register-leak risk equivalent to the traffic-light dots case in the existing principles); (b) on a 390px screen with a non-trivial header + dashboard strip already occupying ~280px above, a growing chat pane forces the user to scroll the main page to see their own typing area, breaking the 'always-visible capture' promise; (c) growth-downward conflicts with the existing top-of-page real estate — every new turn pushes the dashboard cards further down, which is the *opposite* of what should happen on this dashboard.

The brief's gesture toward 'distinct messages vs single pane' frames the choice as a chat-layout problem. It's actually a 'is this chat at all' problem.
findings.user_impact: On mobile, multi-turn coherence (turn 2: 'what about the white one?') only matters if the user can see turn 1 while typing turn 2. With a chat pane that grows downward, the user has to scroll up to remember what they asked, then scroll down to type — at half-attention, in the field, this fails. For Mom: a growing chat pane signals 'this is the kind of app I have to manage,' which fails the leisure-read frame. For desktop Paul: a chat pane is functionally fine but visually wrong on a dashboard.
findings.principle_invoked: Tone-coherence across all chrome (tate-tracker.md); Glyphs follow the journal voice (tate-tracker.md, extended to chrome-shape); Aesthetic & minimalist design (Nielsen H8); Norman — match between system and real world
findings.recommendation:
Replace the 'chat pane' mental model with a 'rolling journal trace' mental model. Concrete:

**The surface always shows: the input field at the top, the last 2-4 turns as plain journal lines below it, no bubbles, no left/right alignment, no avatars, no role labels.** Each turn renders as: timestamp (italic Crimson) · the body text · classification chip if statement · the assistant's reply text if question. Statements and questions look like field-journal entries with optional inline italics for the assistant's response. The visual pattern is 'this is a page of the journal you're writing right now,' not 'this is a conversation.'

**On mobile (390px):** the surface caps at ~3 turns visible by default with a 'show more' link. Older turns scroll within the surface, not within the page — so the dashboard cards below stay where they are. This preserves the dashboard's spatial stability.

**Multi-turn coherence ('what about the white one?') is preserved because the previous turn is visible just below the input** — Paul can SEE turn 1 while typing turn 2. No scrolling required. The session-only Q5 decision is correct; for the assistant's context-window, send the last 3-5 turns.

**Register check:** no message bubbles, no 'You:' / 'Assistant:' labels, no avatar circles, no 'typing...' three-dot animations (use the existing live-indicator pulse pattern from the weather card if a loading state is needed). The chat-app vocabulary stays out of the surface.

findings.observation:
The 'Mom's path' question in the brief gets answered too quickly. The brief's instinct is 'same surface, same voice, the field-journal register is already her register.' That's right for the surface's *output*, but it misses the question of input. Mom in bed with coffee, leisure-reading, is unlikely to *type a question to an AI*. That's a different posture entirely — it requires forming a query, committing to it, waiting for a response, parsing the response, deciding whether to follow up. None of that fits the half-engagement leisure-read context.

The more honest framing: Mom uses the unified surface as a *read surface*, not a *write surface*. She opens the dashboard, sees today-line and/or recent observations Paul saved, scrolls past it. She might never type into it. That's fine. The surface still earns its place for her if (a) it shows her something to read by default (per F3's recommendation re: today-line), (b) it doesn't demand input to be useful, and (c) it doesn't shout at her in a way that breaks the leisure frame.

The risk is the opposite of what the brief frames: not that Mom needs a different mode, but that the surface's *default state* is currently designed as 'a thing you type into' (placeholder text, mic button, save button) — which is wrong for her primary mode of use.
findings.user_impact: If the default empty state of the unified surface is a textarea with placeholder 'What did you see today?' and a mic button, that's an invitation Mom won't accept. She'll see the implicit demand to perform and bounce off — not because the surface is broken, but because the surface's empty state says 'this is for people who do things,' not 'this is for people who notice things.'
findings.principle_invoked: Make every surface read at half-engagement (tate-tracker.md); Mom persona — make-or-break user, leisure-read posture; Tone-coherence
findings.recommendation:
**The empty state of the unified surface is content, not an invitation to perform.** When there's nothing recent in the trace and no today-line yet loaded, the surface shows a journal-voice line — possibly the existing Field Notes intro lifted up, possibly a rotating evocative seed ('Mid-May at Fernwood. The laurel by the spring is opening. Listen for the chorus at dusk.'), possibly the today-line.

The textarea + mic are present but secondary in the empty state — smaller, lower-contrast, with a quieter placeholder ('Note something, or ask the property a question' — content-steward call). The current 'What did you see today?' placeholder is correct for capture-mode but exclusionary for Mom-mode; it presumes she has something to report.

**A defensive move worth considering:** test the surface on Mom with NO typing-mode at all for the first session — just the read-only state. If she opens the app and finds the journal trace alone is enough to keep her returning, then the input is gravy and Paul's the primary user of the write path. If she wants input, she'll ask Paul about it. This is cheaper than designing two modes.

**Critically: do not build a 'Mom mode' toggle.** That's the productivity-app pattern and it's the wrong shape for this. The surface is one surface; what differs is the default state's emphasis.

findings.observation:
Voice-mode flow ambiguity is underspecified. The brief asks: 'on voice-stop, do we auto-send, or wait for explicit send?' This is the wrong binary. There are actually three states the user is in when they stop talking: (a) 'I'm done, send it,' (b) 'I paused, give me a sec,' (c) 'I'm done and I want to read it before sending.' Auto-send eliminates (b) and (c). Wait-for-explicit-send eliminates the speed advantage that's the whole point of voice-in-field.

Separately: the existing Phase D mic implementation has a known UX gap — the user can't tell whether voice-stop happened because they finished or because the browser timed out the recognition session. iOS Safari especially is aggressive about ending recognition after a short silence. Phase E inherits this and it'll be a bigger problem in chat because the user is more likely to think mid-sentence and pause.
findings.user_impact: Paul in the field, voice-dictating 'saw a — uh, what was that bird — a Ruby-throated at the feeder' — current behavior: recognition might cut off at 'uh' and auto-send a fragment, OR it might wait forever and the user has to remember to hit send. Either failure causes him to either save junk or lose the observation entirely.
findings.principle_invoked: User control & freedom (Nielsen H3); Norman — match between system and real world; Friction kills — it just works (cross-project.md, applied to voice)
findings.recommendation:
Three-part:

(1) **Auto-send on voice-stop is wrong as default.** Wait for an explicit Send. The mic-stop transition is the moment to show the transcribed text in the input area with a brief affordance to edit it ('Send' button glows; user can tap mic again to add more, or edit by hand, or send). The cost of waiting is ~1 tap; the cost of mis-sending is losing or corrupting data.

(2) **Differentiate user-stopped from browser-timed-out.** When recognition ends because the browser timed out (no speech for N seconds), the mic button should pulse in a different state (e.g., 'Tap to keep going') instead of reverting to idle. This gives Paul the in-the-field cue that the system stopped listening BUT his text is preserved.

(3) **An explicit 'long-press to dictate, release to stop' alternate input mode for in-field voice** — this is a known pattern from voice memos and message apps and it neatly solves both the auto-send-vs-explicit-send question (release IS the send action, but with a confirmation grace period) and the timeout question (you hold the button so the browser doesn't time out). Worth prototyping as the mobile-primary voice flow even if the standard mic-toggle stays as desktop primary. This is a real Phase E innovation worth the build effort.

findings.observation:
The unified surface needs to disclose what it *is* without explaining itself. The current Phase D surface uses 'Field Notes' as the label and 'What did you see today?' as the placeholder. Phase E inherits the label but the behavior has expanded — it's now both a journal-write surface and a Q&A surface, and the label 'Field Notes' under-promises (sounds write-only) while the placeholder narrows the use case in a way that's now wrong (you can also ASK).

The naming pass the content-steward will handle, but the *affordance* shape needs UX input: how does the surface telegraph 'you can type observations OR questions here' without two buttons, two modes, two placeholders, or an instructional caption (which would violate Friction kills)?
findings.user_impact: First encounter (especially Mom, but also Paul's friends/family who see the dashboard): user sees a textarea with mic, assumes it's for capture, types a question, gets a reply — pleasant surprise. OR: types a question, expects a save, gets confused. The probability of confusion is non-zero and there's no current affordance to set expectations.
findings.principle_invoked: Recognition rather than recall (Nielsen H6); Friction kills (cross-project.md); Norman — signifiers
findings.recommendation:
Two moves, used together:

(1) **Placeholder text carries the dual mode.** 'Note something, or ask the property a question.' (Content-steward final call.) The placeholder is the only instruction the surface offers, and the placeholder IS journal-voice — 'ask the property' frames the assistant as a knowing-thing rather than an AI tool, which holds the field-journal frame. Avoid 'Type or dictate anything…' (the brief's suggestion) — too generic, doesn't telegraph the two modes.

(2) **The first-turn trace teaches the modes by demonstration.** The first time a user types a statement, the saved-entry trace appears (per F2). The first time they type a question, the reply appears in journal-voice italic. After 2-3 mixed turns, the user has a mental model of what the surface does without ever being told.

This is the 'show, don't tell' affordance pattern — it relies on the surface's empty state being safe to experiment with (no destructive action on any path) and on the routing visibility (F1) being good enough that the user trusts each turn's outcome.

**Naming pass — flag for content-steward but UX-relevant:** 'Field Notes' is currently both the section label and the card-below label. With Phase E, the top surface is bigger than just notes. Possible names: 'The Almanac' (matches the header subtitle 'An Appalachian Almanac'), 'Today at Fernwood,' 'The Property' (one word, journal-voice), or no name at all (let the surface be unlabeled, supported by the placeholder and trace). The 'no name' option is worth pushing on — naming a surface is a productivity-app habit that may not earn its place here.
findings.effort: low (placeholder + naming decision); medium if 'no name' chosen and other labels need to adjust

findings.observation: The brief's 'error / uncertainty path' is voiced beautifully ('looks like it could be lacebug damage — I'd want to see the underside of a leaf to be sure'). But the *system-error* paths are underspecified — Worker offline, classifier returns malformed JSON, the conversation hits the context limit, the user's network drops mid-dictation. In Phase D's current implementation, classify failures are silent (per the code: 'failures are silent'). That's correct for Phase D because the entry still saves. In Phase E it's wrong: if the question path fails silently, the user sees nothing happen, has no reply, doesn't know whether to retry.
findings.user_impact: Paul in the field, voice-dictates a question, network drops, no reply ever appears. He has no cue. He waits, gets impatient, types it again — possibly accidentally creating a duplicate observation if the second attempt is classified as a statement. Or he assumes the assistant doesn't know and moves on, losing the inquiry. For Mom: a silent failure on her first attempted question is the most likely 'I'm done with this app' moment.
findings.principle_invoked: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors (Nielsen H9); Caution as noticing, not warning (tate-tracker.md, applied to error voice)
findings.recommendation:
Every system-failure mode needs a visible, in-voice cue in the surface:

(1) **Network/Worker failure on send:** the trace area shows the user's input as a journal line but in muted color, with a quiet inline note in italic ('Couldn't reach the property — try again') and a 'Retry' text-link. NOT a red error banner. The voice matches the existing field-journal register; the failure is a noticing, not a warning. Existing principle 'Caution as noticing, not warning' applies one level deeper than it has before.

(2) **Classifier failure (statement path):** the entry still saves (current Phase D behavior is correct), but the category chip area shows a quiet 'uncategorized — tap to set' affordance instead of staying blank. This avoids the journal silently accumulating entries with no category.

(3) **Context-limit exhaustion (multi-turn):** the surface needs a quiet 'starting fresh' moment when the conversation gets long enough that older turns are being truncated. The journal-voice version: 'Earlier in the conversation, you asked about the azaleas. From here, we're starting a new page.' This is the field-journal version of 'context cleared,' and it gives the user a mental model of why the assistant might not remember earlier turns.

(4) **The 'I don't know about this property' case** (the brief's good example) is the *content* path, not a system error — that one is content-steward's territory and the brief handles it well. Flagging the distinction: system errors and uncertainty are two different failure modes that should look different in the surface. System errors are recoverable (retry), uncertainty is not (the model genuinely doesn't know).

findings.observation:
Accessibility — voice dictation + screen-reader compatibility. The brief asks for this. Three real issues:

(a) **Live regions for async content.** When the assistant's reply streams in (if it streams) or appears after a delay, a screen reader needs an `aria-live` region to announce it. The current Phase D implementation has no aria-live; Phase E inherits and amplifies this gap (a reply landing silently in the DOM is invisible to AT).

(b) **Voice-dictation conflict with screen-reader announcements.** Both consume the audio channel — when the user has VoiceOver on and uses the mic, the screen reader's announcements compete with their own dictation. This is a known iOS issue; the standard accommodation is to pause screen-reader output while dictation is active, but the Web Speech API doesn't broker this. The mic button needs a clear focused state and a tactile/visual cue (the existing red-pulse 'recording' state) that doesn't depend on the audio channel.

(c) **Focus management across turns.** After send, where does keyboard focus go? If it stays in the textarea (which has cleared), screen-reader users have no way to hear the reply unless they manually navigate. Focus should move to the new trace line on send, then return to the textarea on next focus action.
findings.user_impact: Mom uses iPhone, may use Accessibility shortcuts (larger text, possibly VoiceOver if her eyesight changes). Paul tests the app in real-world conditions and may use voice in noisy environments where screen-reader audio doubles up. Both cases break under the current Phase D implementation and Phase E will inherit unless designed in.
findings.principle_invoked: Norman — feedback (audio + visual + tactile, not single-channel); WCAG 2.1 — name/role/value, focus order, status messages; Nielsen H1 visibility extended to assistive technology
findings.recommendation:
Three concrete moves (engineering-partner will own the implementation; UX-relevant decisions are):

(1) **Wrap the trace area in `aria-live='polite' aria-atomic='false'`.** New turns get announced. Statement-save traces get a screen-reader-only prefix like 'Saved: ' so the AT user knows what kind of event landed.

(2) **Move focus to the most recent trace line on send.** Keyboard users can tab back to the input by hitting Shift+Tab once. This is standard chat-app focus management adapted to the journal-voice context.

(3) **Mic recording state needs three-channel feedback:** visual (the existing red pulse), color (button changes hue), and label (`aria-label` flips from 'Voice dictation' to 'Stop dictation, listening now' — which the current implementation gets right). DO NOT add audio chime for start/stop — that conflicts with VoiceOver. The visual+aria channel suffices.

**Out-of-scope flag for ax-specific expert:** if Paul wants a deeper a11y review later, that's a different specialist. This finding flags the highest-leverage issues a UX expert can catch without diving into ARIA implementation.

findings.observation:
Holistic register check across the unified surface. Pulling from the existing principles library: the new surface needs to pass Tone-coherence and Glyphs-follow-the-journal-voice on every micro-element. Three places to watch in build:

(a) **The send button.** A green gradient 'Save entry' button is what Phase D ships. For Phase E, with the surface routing to multiple outcomes, the button label question is real ('Save'? 'Send'? 'Note it'?). The current 'Save entry' is wrong for question-mode. Probably the button stays a quiet send-glyph or a single word like 'Note' — content-steward call, but flag that the button can't say 'Save entry' anymore.

(b) **The 'classifying...' state.** Phase D shows 'classifying…' italic gray under entries while async classification runs. That label is honest but borrows from the wrong register — it announces the AI machinery. The journal-voice version: nothing visible, OR a tiny three-dot pulse (the existing live-indicator pattern from Weather card) without a label. Let the chip appear when ready; don't narrate the wait.

(c) **The mic recording state.** Current Phase D mic button changes to ■ when recording. That's a stop glyph from media-player vocabulary. It's fine but it's a register-leak candidate worth a second look — possible alternatives: the mic glyph itself turns red and pulses (no glyph change), or the mic gets replaced with a wave-form animation. Minor compared to F1-F9 but worth noting before build hardens the pattern.
findings.user_impact: Each one is small. Together they're the slow accretion of register-leak that 'Glyphs follow the journal voice' was written to prevent. Mom won't articulate 'this feels like an admin panel' — she'll just open it less.
findings.principle_invoked: Tone-coherence across all chrome (tate-tracker.md); Glyphs follow the journal voice (tate-tracker.md); Ornament earns its place (cross-project.md)
findings.recommendation: Do a once-over of every micro-element in the surface before build — button labels, loading states, status chips, glyph choices — against the journal-voice register. The cross-project 'Icons earn their place — true AND useful' rule and the tate-tracker 'Glyphs follow the journal voice' rule together should catch most of this; the new pieces are (a) the button label (b) the classify-pending state.

open_questions_for_user: Does today-line get folded INTO the unified surface as the initial state, or does it stay where it is and the surface starts with a lifted journal-intro empty state? (F3 / F5)

Will Mom actually try to type into the unified surface, or is she a read-only user of it? Worth a direct conversation with her on her next visit / call. If she's read-only, the surface can lean into that explicitly and the input becomes Paul's territory. (F5)
Is the 'long-press to dictate' alternate mobile voice input flow worth Phase E build effort, or defer to a later refinement? (F6)
Is the unified surface's *name* a thing Paul wants to design now, or hold for after the surface ships? My read: hold, observe what people call it in conversation. (F7)

Multi-turn coherence ceiling — when does the assistant 'start a new page'? After N turns, after M minutes of idle, on explicit user action, or never (always-context until truncation forces it)? UX recommends a visible 'starting fresh' moment regardless of trigger (F8).
follow_up_research_suggested: Once Phase E ships: log the misclassification rate in real use (statement misrouted as question, question misrouted as statement). If >10%, the F1 recommendations need to harden into pre-commit confirmation; if <5%, the visibility-only fix is sufficient.

First-week observation: does Mom open the unified surface? Does she scroll past it? Does she ever type into it? This is the F5 validation path and it should be a deliberate behavioral check, not assumed.

Voice-mode timing study: in the field with Paul, observe 10-20 real dictation events. How often does the browser time out mid-thought? How often does Paul want to pause and continue? This validates or invalidates the F6 long-press recommendation.

After 30+ turns of real use across both users: is the 'rolling journal trace' pattern (F4) reading as a journal or as a chat? If it reads as chat, the register-leak is real and the surface needs visual moves to push it back toward journal.

principles_to_propose.principle: Visibility of routing decisions in unified surfaces
principles_to_propose.rationale: Phase E surfaces a class of UX problem the existing principles library doesn't directly cover: when an interface accepts ambiguous input and routes it to one of several outcomes (statement → save, question → reply, ambiguous → both), the user needs visibility into the routing decision AT the moment it commits — not just into the final outcome. This is a Nielsen H1 (visibility of system state) application that gets sharper when applied specifically to AI-driven intent classification. Worth distilling into a principle because Bolo Boys will likely face the same pattern as soon as it has any AI-mediated UX (e.g., a chat bot on the band site, or AI-assisted booking forms). Draft statement: 'When a surface accepts ambiguous input and routes it to one of several outcomes, the routing decision must be visible in the surface as it commits — not just the final outcome. Silent routing erodes trust the first time it's wrong.'

principles_to_propose.principle: Empty states are content, not invitations to perform
principles_to_propose.scope: tate-tracker (initial); candidate for promotion if it generalizes
principles_to_propose.rationale: F5 surfaced this in a sharper form than the existing principles capture. The empty state of any Tate Tracker surface should give the user something to read — a quiet evocative line, an inviting fact about the property, a today-line — not just a textarea with placeholder text. This holds the Mom-mode leisure-read context. Existing 'Meet the user at the action' (cross-project) covers the related but distinct case of confirmation/result screens; it doesn't cover empty states. Draft statement: 'An empty state must give the user something to read or notice — never just a prompt to perform. The user opening a surface in leisure-read mode (Tate Tracker) or first-encounter mode (any project) finds an invitation to act exclusionary if they had no intent to act.' Worth checking against Bolo Boys empty states before promoting.

principles_to_propose.principle: AI machinery stays out of the surface's voice
principles_to_propose.rationale: F10 (and several findings across F1-F8) keep landing on the same point: every place the AI feature announces itself in the UI (loading states like 'classifying...', error messages like 'Claude returned malformed JSON', mode toggles like 'Save vs Ask'), it leaks the AI machinery into the user's frame. The remedy isn't to hide that the surface uses AI — it's to keep the AI's voice (loading, error, uncertainty) in the project's voice. Tate Tracker → field-journal voice. Bolo Boys → band's voice. The principle isn't 'hide AI,' it's 'AI speaks the project's register.' Draft statement: 'When a surface is AI-mediated, the AI's machinery — loading states, intermediate processing, error modes, mode-switches — speaks in the surface's voice, not in the platform's default vocabulary. The user should never have to know AI is involved to use the surface; the user should also never have to read 'classifying' or 'reasoning' or 'request failed' in the surface's own voice channel.'
